title: S3 Deep Dive: Storage Classes, Lifecycle & Security

scenes.narration: S 3 questions are the densest concentration of sounds-right-but-is-wrong traps on both the associate and the professional exam. On the associate exam, this chapter's material is graded against two domains that together make up half the score: designing secure architectures at thirty percent — the single largest domain on the entire exam — and designing cost-optimized architectures at twenty percent. One number worth anchoring on right away: the default number of buckets you get per account today is ten thousand, raised from just one hundred back in November of twenty twenty-four. If older material tells you one hundred, that's stale, not current.

props.title: S3 Deep Dive: Storage Classes, Lifecycle & Security

scenes.narration: Three instincts trip candidates up over and over, and each one feels reasonable in the moment. On storage class: Standard is the default, storage is cheap, so just put everything there and stop analyzing the access pattern. On access control: I need one specific principal to read one specific object, so I'll attach an access control list — spelled out, an A C L — straight onto that object; it feels precise and surgical. And on encryption: the bucket already has encryption at rest turned on, so the data is secure, and who's allowed to call the A P I is a secondary concern. Every one of these optimizes for the one dimension you can see immediately, while ignoring the dimension the question is actually testing.

props.heading: "Leave it in Standard, lock it down with an ACL"
bullets: Storage class: 'Standard is the default and storage is cheap — just put everything there.'
Access control: 'I need one principal to read one object, so attach an ACL directly to it.'
Encryption: 'The bucket has encryption at rest on, so the data is secure — access control is secondary.'

scenes.narration: Here's the mechanism behind each trap. S3 Standard carries no retrieval fee and no minimum storage duration, which is exactly right for data read constantly — but it's a real, measurable cost penalty for anything read rarely, since the cheaper tiers exist precisely to trade a lower storage price for a retrieval fee and a duration commitment. Access control lists are grants attached per object, with no central place to audit who can read what across a bucket holding millions of objects — Amazon's own current guidance is to avoid them almost entirely in favor of bucket or I AM policies. And encryption at rest protects the bytes sitting on disk; it does nothing to stop a principal with an overly broad policy from calling GetObject through the normal API and getting the decrypted plaintext back, because S3 decrypts transparently for any authorized request. Storage class, encryption, and access control are three separate levers — the exam expects you to reach for the right one, not the most familiar one.

props.heading: One control, one axis — never the whole picture
bullets: Standard has no retrieval fee and no minimum duration — right for hot data, a real cost penalty for anything read rarely.
ACLs are per-object grants with no central place to audit access across millions of objects — AWS's own guidance is to avoid them.
Encryption protects bytes on disk; it does nothing to stop an over-permissioned principal from calling GetObject and getting the plaintext.

scenes.narration: Walk the decision the way the exam actually poses it — starting from what you know about the access pattern, not from a list of names to memorize. If access is frequent and predictable, Standard is correct: no retrieval fee, no minimum duration, millisecond reads. If the access pattern is genuinely unknown or changes over time, the answer is Intelligent-Tiering — it monitors each object and moves it automatically, with no retrieval fee charged for those automatic moves, which is exactly why guessing between Standard and an infrequent-access tier is the wrong move here. If access is known to be infrequent but still needs a millisecond read when it happens, you're choosing between Standard-IA and One Zone-IA — both carry a real per-gigabyte retrieval fee and roughly a thirty-day minimum storage duration, with One Zone-IA trading away cross-availability-zone redundancy for a lower price. And for true archival, where retrieval time itself is negotiable, you pick a Glacier tier by how long you can tolerate waiting — not just by the word 'archive.'

props.heading: The real storage-class decision tree
steps: Frequent, predictable access → S3 Standard — no retrieval fee, no minimum duration
Unknown or changing access pattern → Intelligent-Tiering — auto-tiers, zero fee on the moves
Known infrequent, still needs millisecond reads → Standard-IA / One Zone-IA — fee + ~30-day minimum
Archival, retrieval time is negotiable → pick the Glacier tier by tolerance for delay

scenes.narration: Put every class side by side and four facts are almost everything the exam tests. Durability is eleven nines across every class except One Zone-infrequent-access, because durability comes from replication across multiple availability zones — One Zone trades that away for a lower price. What actually changes class to class is access-frequency fit, minimum storage duration, and retrieval time. Standard and Intelligent-Tiering carry no minimum duration and no retrieval fee at all. Standard-infrequent-access and One Zone-infrequent-access both carry roughly a thirty-day minimum and a real per-gigabyte fee. And the three Glacier tiers layer on longer minimums still — ninety, ninety, and one hundred eighty days — with retrieval time stretching from milliseconds for Instant Retrieval, to minutes-or-hours for Flexible Retrieval depending on request speed, to hours for Deep Archive, which is also the cheapest to store.

props.heading: Access fit, duration, and retrieval time in one table

scenes.narration: Encryption follows the same 'which one satisfies the constraint' logic as storage class. With no special requirement stated, S S E-S3 is correct: AWS manages the keys entirely, zero configuration, and it's on by default for every bucket today. If the scenario needs an audit trail of every single decrypt, or a key-level access policy independent of the bucket, that's S S E-K M S — every use of that key gets logged to CloudTrail, and the key carries its own policy. If the requirement is that you supply and control the actual encryption key yourself, with AWS never persisting it, that's S S E-C: you send the key with every request, S3 uses it once, and doesn't keep it. And if AWS must never see the plaintext or the key at all, you reach for client-side encryption — encrypting before the object ever leaves your application. These are ordered by how much you're willing to manage yourself, not by how secure each one sounds.

props.kicker: MATCH THE CONSTRAINT TO THE OPTION
props.heading: Four encryption options, four different guarantees

cells: AWS manages keys entirely, zero config, on by default
Audit trail of every decrypt + key-level policy
Every use logged to CloudTrail; key has its own policy
You supply/control the key, AWS never stores it
You send the key each request; S3 uses it once, discards it
AWS must never see plaintext or key at all
Encrypted before it ever leaves your application

scenes.narration: Four documents anchor a compliant, cost-optimized bucket, and you won't be asked to write them from scratch on a multiple-choice exam — you'll be shown one and asked what it actually does. A lifecycle policy file drives multi-stage storage-class transitions and an expiration rule. A bucket policy denies access by default and allows it only from one V P C endpoint and one role. An encryption config sets default S S E-K M S with a customer-managed key. And a public-access-block document turns on all four Block Public Access settings at once. Reading these correctly — recognizing what's present and what's conspicuously missing — is the actual skill being tested.

props.kicker: THE DOCUMENTS THE EXAM EXPECTS YOU TO RECOGNIZE
props.heading: reference-bucket-config/
lines: ├── bucket-policy.json        # deny-by-default, allow only a VPC endpoint + one role
├── encryption-config.json    # default SSE-KMS with a customer-managed key
└── public-access-block.json  # all four Block Public Access settings enabled

scenes.narration: This is the single most exam-relevant table in the chapter, because it resolves the fights the other tools can't. A bucket policy is one JSON document that governs the whole bucket — the exam-favored answer whenever the question is really about controlling access to one bucket, especially across accounts or from one VPC endpoint. An I AM policy attaches to a principal and follows it across every bucket it touches — reach for this when the constraint is really about what an application role or a team can do, not about one bucket. An ACL is a legacy, per-object grant with no central audit view — almost never the right new-design answer. And Block Public Access is the override: an account- or bucket-level switch that beats any policy or ACL that would otherwise allow public access, which is exactly why it's the correct answer whenever a scenario says a bucket must never become public, even by accident.

props.heading: Access control: which mechanism actually wins

rows.label: Bucket policy
cells: One auditable, centrally-managed rule — cross-account, VPC-endpoint-only

rows.label: IAM policy
cells: Attached to a principal, every bucket it touches
The constraint is about what a role or team can do everywhere

rows.label: ACL (legacy)
cells: Almost never — AWS's own guidance says avoid it

rows.label: Block Public Access
cells: Overrides any policy or ACL that would allow public access

scenes.narration: Three commands, run in the order that actually matters — lock it down before you open it up. First, put-public-access-block, turning on all four Block Public Access settings before any policy exists, so no later policy mistake can ever accidentally expose the bucket. Second, put-bucket-encryption, setting default encryption to S S E-K M S with a customer-managed key — chosen here because this design needs the CloudTrail audit trail, not out of habit. Third, put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration, which applies a rule that ages current objects from Standard into infrequent access at day thirty, into Glacier at day ninety, and expires them at day three sixty-five, while aging old object versions out even faster. Notice what's deliberately absent from this sequence: no ACL command anywhere.

props.heading: Lock it down, then open exactly what's needed

output: BlockPublicAcls, IgnorePublicAcls, BlockPublicPolicy, RestrictPublicBuckets: all true
Customer-managed key applied to all new objects.

scenes.narration: Run this one through the framework by hand. Meridian Streamworks hosts several million video clips. Most go cold after their first month online — but any single clip can unpredictably go viral months or years later and need fast, frequent access again for a few days, with no human watching to reclassify it. That's not a 'pick Standard or infrequent-access' question at all — it's the textbook unknown-or-changing access pattern this chapter's decision tree was built around. The answer is Intelligent-Tiering: it monitors each object's access and moves it automatically, with no retrieval fee charged for those automatic moves, so a viral clip gets fast access back without anyone having predicted it in advance.

props.heading: Meridian Streamworks — millions of clips, one unpredictable pattern

profile.name: Meridian Streamworks
profile.role: Several million video assets · most go cold after 30 days · any clip can go viral again, unpredictably
profile.detail: Most clips are never watched again after their first month online — except that any clip can unpredictably 'go viral' months or years later and suddenly need fast, frequent access for a few days. Meridian wants the lowest sustainable cost with no human re-classifying objects by hand.
profile.verdict: S3 Intelligent-Tiering — the textbook unknown-or-changing access pattern; a manual Standard-IA or Glacier assignment would either overpay on hot data or eat retrieval fees exactly when a clip goes viral.

scenes.narration: Try these yourself before we reveal the answers. First: an object transitions from Standard into Standard-infrequent-access on day zero, then gets deleted on day twelve — what actually happens on the bill? Second, a professional-level one: a compliance team needs to prove exactly which principal decrypted a given object and when, and wants to revoke one application's decrypt access without touching the bucket policy at all — which encryption option delivers that on its own?

questions.prompt: An object transitions from Standard into Standard-IA on day 0, then is deleted on day 12. What happens on the bill?
options: Nothing extra — billed only for the 12 days it existed in Standard-IA
Billed as if it stayed the full minimum storage duration (roughly 30 days), even though it was deleted on day 12
S3 blocks the deletion until the minimum duration has passed
The retrieval fee is waived since the object was deleted, not read

questions.prompt: A compliance team needs to prove which principal decrypted an object and when, and to revoke one application's decrypt access without touching the bucket policy. Which encryption option delivers this on its own?
options: Any option — S3 logs all access equally regardless of encryption choice

scenes.narration: Here's why. Standard-infrequent-access and One Zone-infrequent-access both carry a real minimum storage duration — roughly thirty days — and deleting or transitioning out early doesn't stop that clock. S3 doesn't block the deletion, and there's no retrieval fee here since nothing was read; you simply end up paying the minimum-duration rate for far less benefit than planned. And for the audit-trail question, S S E-K M S with a customer-managed key is the only option that delivers both halves on its own: every decrypt against that key is logged to CloudTrail, and the key carries an access policy independent of the bucket, so revoking one application's access becomes a key-policy change, not a bucket-policy change. S S E-S3 gives no comparable per-key audit trail, and S S E-C shifts key management onto the caller with no built-in logging of its own.

answers.prompt: An object transitions into Standard-IA on day 0, then is deleted on day 12.
answers.correct: Billed as if it stayed the full ~30-day minimum, even though it was deleted on day 12.
answers.rationale: Standard-IA and One Zone-IA both carry a real minimum storage duration commitment. Deleting or transitioning out early doesn't stop that clock — S3 doesn't block the deletion, and there's no retrieval fee involved since nothing was read; you simply pay the minimum-duration rate for less benefit than planned.

answers.prompt: Prove per-object who decrypted what, and revoke one application's access independently.
answers.rationale: Every decrypt against a KMS key is logged to CloudTrail, and the key carries its own access policy separate from the bucket — so revoking one application's access is a key-policy change, not a bucket-policy change. SSE-S3 gives no comparable per-key audit trail, and SSE-C has no built-in audit trail either — it just shifts key management onto the caller.

scenes.narration: Five things to carry forward. An unknown or changing access pattern points at Intelligent-Tiering, not a guess between Standard and an infrequent-access tier. Infrequent-access and Glacier tiers carry a real minimum storage duration and a real per-gigabyte retrieval fee — cheap storage is never the same as free storage. Bucket policies and I AM policies are today's recommended access-control tools; access control lists are legacy, and Block Public Access overrides every one of them when it's enabled. Encryption at rest and access control are independent controls — S S E-K M S buys you an audit trail, not a substitute for a correctly scoped policy. And the default bucket quota is ten thousand per account today, but a bucket-per-tenant design is still the wrong pattern no matter how big that number gets. Next: S3's durability guarantees nothing about keeping a compute fleet available — chapter seven covers Elastic Load Balancing and Auto Scaling, the mechanisms that keep an application up while EC2 instances come and go underneath it.

props.heading: What to remember from this chapter
takeaways: Unknown or changing access pattern → Intelligent-Tiering, not a guess between Standard and an infrequent-access tier.
IA and Glacier tiers carry a real minimum storage duration and a real per-GB retrieval fee — cheap storage isn't free storage.
Bucket and IAM policies are the current recommended access-control tools; ACLs are legacy, and Block Public Access overrides all of them.
Encryption at rest and access control are independent controls — SSE-KMS buys an audit trail, not a substitute for a correct policy.
The default bucket quota is 10,000 per account today, but bucket-per-tenant is still the wrong pattern regardless of the number.

scenes.narration: One more to work through yourself. A compliance archive needs to be retrievable within twelve hours if it's ever needed, gets read at most once or twice a year, and must prove exactly who decrypted it and when. Using this chapter's two decision trees — one for storage class, one for encryption — which class and which encryption option actually fit? And here's the trap worth naming out loud: why would Glacier Deep Archive, the cheapest option on the table, be the wrong pick here even though 'rarely read' sounds like its exact use case?

props.prompt: A compliance archive must be retrievable within 12 hours if ever needed, is read once or twice a year at most, and must prove who decrypted it and when. Which storage class and encryption option fit — and why is Glacier Deep Archive, the cheapest option, still the wrong pick?
props.hint: Two separate decision trees apply — one for storage class, one for encryption — and the correct answer isn't the cheapest one on either.
